On the orders of the day:
Mr. CAMERON R. McINTOSH (North Battleford):	I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon). I have received information from northern Saskatchewan to the effect that certain soldier settlers cannot procure seed or feed oats. Last year the seed apparently was received too late and there was no crop. This year the same situation will occur if something is not done. I understand that the men concerned have appealed to the municipality, to the soldier settlement board, to the Canadian Legion, and as well to the minister. May I ask whether the minister will be good enough to investigate these cases immediately and to take remedial action on behalf of these men who are in dire need of seed and feed oats.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: So far as I am aware, no communication has been addressed to the director of soldier settlement in connection with the matter to which the hon. gentleman refers. I do not know whether my hon. friend is willing to let me have the names of the soldier settlers who complain, but it would facilitate investigation of the matter if I had them.

Yes; I shall be willing
to give the name I have here.
Is the federal government giving anything in the way of feed or seed oats to the people on the prairies? I did not know that was being done.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The federal government in the past has loaned money to the provinces for that purpose and I believe in some instances seed has been supplied to soldier settlers, although I may be wrong in that regard. The director of soldier settlement has advised me that there are very few cases where soldier settlers are in need of seed. I will inquire further into the matter to see to what extent, if any, seed has been supplied to soldier settlers. Generally speaking, where it became apparent that the settler, not under soldier settlement, was unable to supply the seed himself and the province could not supply it, a loan has been made, as indicated and discussed in this house, to the province for the purpose of providing seed in certain areas.

subtopic: CONDITION OF SETTLERS IN ROUYN DISTRICT
speechtext:
When the house learns why the telegram has been sent collect I do not think anyone will laugh. Everyone recalls an article written by the correspondent of the Toronto Globe, who made the statement that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) showed great incredulity when I cited some cases of distress in the colonization district. The following telegram comes from the district of Rouyn:
3.40 p.m., April 25, 1933.
Jean-Frangois Pouliot,
Ottawa.
N'avons plus rien a manger.
"We have nothing more to eat."
Je vous demande d'interpeller le gouverne-ment pour nous.
"I ask you to make representations to the government on our behalf."
Sinon il y aura des mortalites.
"Otherwise people will die."
Settlers in Rouyn District

Lettre suit.
"Letter follows."
Agissez avant qu'il soit trop tard.
"Act before it is too late."
(Signd) Marcel Essiambre.
I have not yet received that letter. Now, when an aviator is lost or not heard from the government is ready to spend hundreds of thousands of dollars to find him, and I do not see why this or any other government should not be prepared to come at once to the rescue of these people. Surely it should not be a matter of corresponding with this one or that one. As I say, when an aviator is lost in the fog or at sea, this government dispatches searching parties to rescue him. I have been laughed at because I have brought to the attention of the house certain cases of distress in this country, settlers who were left far away in the wilderness without any means of sustaining themselves. In connection with the situation I am now discussing I have some letters which I will give to the house. I regret that I have not the translation ready but I will give the letters in French and ask the Minister of Labour to be good enough to instruct the chief translator to submit a translation to him as early as possible. I would ask him to get the translation as soon as it is printed on Monday next. Here is the first letter I have:
Les Etroits, April 19, 1933. Mr. Jean-Frangois Pouliot,
Member for Temiscouata.
Dear Sir,-
I am writing to you a few lines to inform you how things are managed here. We are at the point of starvation. I am appealing to you for funds to purchase food. As to direct assistance, it was impossible to obtain any during the whole winter. I was paid $12 for work done, and $14 was allotted to the whole of my family. You may judge for yourself what hardships we endured throughout the winter.
For Heaven's sake, are you not able to get us $75 to do our seeding. I depend on you for a livelihood.
Another letter I received from the parish of St. Louis du Ha! Ha!, county of Temiscouata; reads as follows:
St. Louis du Ha! Ha!
February 25, 1933.
Mr. Jean-Frangois Pouliot.
Sir,-
_ I am appealing to you, to-day, to grant us, for God's sake a small contribution. Like every one here, I am in great distress. I had purchased a horse for $195, and I had almost completed my payments, being only $5 short; however, the man who sold me the horse would not wait any longer, he came to get his horse. T cannot find the money to pay a first instal-

ment on another. I am disheartened, not having earned any money this winter. I worked for a Mr. Couturier and I was only paid in goods. My wife, who is in poor health, is greatly discouraged. I wonder what will be the end.
A horse is indispensible on a farm, and during these hard years my farm has not given sufficient returns to enable me to save. I still owe $500 on the farm and I am doing my best to keep it out of liquidation. Last autumn I ploughed quite a large patch of land, sufficient to sow all I required in order to live without too much hardship; however, not having any horses, I shall be unable to sow what I ploughed.
If you could send me a small amount or make me a small loan, at not too high a rate of interest, 1 would be very grateful to you. You are aware that things have changed, to-day, the Liberals have nothing to do with the Conservative administration. Had I belonged to the same party as the man who sold me the horse, perhaps, he would have been lenient towards me. I beg of you, for God's sake, to kindly grant or advance me a small amount, for a few years, on a promissory note, at not too high a rate of interest.
I have no means of purchasing a horse. Times are hard, especially for farmers whose lands are not yet paid in full. I am aware that I shall not forfeit my farm providing I meet the interest on what is owed. I am very grateful to an old relative who is kind enough to help me.
Kindly, sir, accede, if possible, to my request, my wife and myself would be very grateful to you, and, should it meet with your wishes, we should be glad to have you pay us a visit next time you come to St. Louis. Thanking you in anticipation, etc., etc.
The following is another letter, sir.
Biencourt, April 3, 1933. Mr. Jean-Frangois Pouliot.
Sir,-
You will pardon me if I take the liberty of writing to you. I should appreciate a few suggestions from you and, at the same time, I wish to inform you how we fared throughout the winter in our dear parish of Biencourt. I have been residing here since October 13, 1931. I came to settle here as I could not earn a livelihood in my own parish. I therefore undertook farming in earnest, as new settlers we did fairly well, so far as clearing the land and	doing	other odd jobs,	especiallyas no forest	fires	had devastated	the	land.
However, our crop was practically nil, except for a little straw.
We were, therefore, not in the best of circumstances to	begin	the winter; the	first	dayswe cut 38 cords of	pulpwood at $3	per	cord.
I was able to set aside 50 cents per cord, the balance having been seized for an old debt. The company carted away the wood at the rate of 90 cents per cord; however, I was unable to draw the balance of my money. I wish to inquire whether this is practicable. That is all the money I was able to draw-with the exception of $40 which I earned last autumn-[DOT] to provide for a family of ten during the whole winter. These are certainly hard times, no potatoes or other food, except bread and meat obtained through hunting. Had the latter not

Settlers in Rouyn District
been so plentiful, we would have been forced to feed on grass.
There still remains the question of clothes. Many of these are badly worn, especially boots.
Would you, therefore, kindly inform me what steps should be taken to recover what is coming to me. We have heard that the government's timber-cut was not seizable, etc.
He continues:
I did not remain inactive, I ploughed 7 acres for the spring which, however, I shall be unable to sow. I have neither seed grain nor money. We could have sown more last spring, but we *were unable to obtain more than three bags of seed grain and then we had to undertake three trips, at 10 miles distance, to obtain them. I am preparing 10 more acres for next spring. I have begun to build a barn, 36 feet by 40 feet, all the work was done with an axe; I also have some shingles which I, myself, made with a drawing-knife. I wish to follow the good example set by my old father.
I trust that it will not give you too much trouble to answer my letter at your earliest convenience.
An lion. MEMBER: Carried.

subtopic: CONDITION OF SETTLERS IN ROUYN DISTRICT
speechtext:
When people are suffering there should not be jokes made about their misery. I regret I have to do what I am doing but I do it because people are suffering. If these people were being looked after in accordance with the famous Gordon plan, I would not have received any of these letters. I might tell my hon. friend that I stopped at a house in his county. There were three men out of work and they told me they were being forced to live upon bread and molasses. One of the men was an able carpenter and he had to fill in his time by fishing. Another man was a good mason and he had to go wild duck hunting. The third man could not get any work at all. Those are the conditions which existed in one home in the constituency of my hon. friend. I have always tried to be courteous to him but I feel that jokes should not be made about the misery of these people. My hon. friend claims that these conditions do not exist but I will not waste the time of the house any more. Let him remain quiet in his seat while others defend the poor people who are suffering.
Les Etroits, April 7, 1933. Mr. J. F. I'ouliot,
Ottawa.
Mr. Pouliot,-
I have been very unfortunate these days. I had a team of good horses to work my land; both died within a month. . . .

one. I would ask you, sir, to request the sergeant at arms to escort him from the chamber.
I regret the disturbance from the other side of the house but I may tell my hon. friends that they will not prevent me from saying all that I have to say. I am not saying this for the benefit of either the government or the Liberal party, I am speaking on behalf of the poor people who have to suffer. Onions are food; the hon.

subtopic: CONDITION OF SETTLERS IN ROUYN DISTRICT
speechtext:
The letter continues:
I have been very unfortunate these days. I had a team of good horses to work my land; both died within a month; as you are aware, one is not master of his destiny. I find it impossible to purchase a horse this spring to carry on my seeding.
I have not earned anything within the last two years. We had to practise thrift in order to live on the small returns which this land brings.
I have been married ten years and have eight children. I have received no assistance and found it impossible to leave the house and take up unemployment work. Each time unemployment work started, it was impossible for me to go and work, my wife was ill, moreover, the work was being done at a distance from my house-it was therefore impossible to leave the house. I never received any bonus for clearing my land because I happened to be on a patented lot.
I am, therefore, obliged to beg of you some little assistance to purchase a horse; perhaps, some of your friends will subscribe. I am one of your electors and so are all my relations, as you are aware.
I wish to thank you for the information given in connection with the road fence.
St. Emile-d'Auclair,
March 26, 1933.
Mr. J. F. Pouliot,
Mr. Pouliot,-
Just a few lines to inquire how the Unemployment Act affects the settlers of Auclair. I settled on my lot last October and have not received any assistance, while some folks who have been here for a year, have received $32 per family, and the boys $20; others received assistance to build themselves a camp. Must one hail from the city to be given assistance? I am a farmer's son having lived in the country and always tilled the land, I would,
Settlers in Rouyn District

therefore, like to be encouraged as others, because if things do not improve, there will be great distress; we, from the county of Temiscouata, have not been treated as fairly as the people from Lac-Noir or elsewhere.
Please, inquire from Messrs	
of St. Hubert, who are aware of this fact.
Packington, March 29, 1933.
Mr. J. F. Pouliot,
Member for Temiscouata,
House of Commons.
Dear Sir,-
1 wish to apprise you of our condition. We are men from your county and have come to the conclusion that you have the courage and backbone to espouse our cause. Do everything possible to obtain a little food for us, at least for our children. We are ready to take our oath on what we shall disclose to you. We are entirely devoid of food, clothes and implements.
Our horses have died of hunger and it will not be long before some of us meet the same fate. We were forced to sell oUr live stock at ridiculous prices, they had cost us very dear. How do you expect us to work when we are practically naked, without clothes, food or implements? Yet, if we do not work we will be looked upon as lazy and good for nothing.
Last spring we resorted to oxen so as to harrow the land; however, we had to sacrifice them. If you cannot obtain any help from the government, could you not possibly raise a subscription among the members or ministers.
For Heaven sake, Mr. Pouliot, do try and arrange matters so that an inquiry may be held on the spot.
It is impossible to describe our situation, such as it is; however, please endeavour to collect a few cents to buy bread for our little children and wives. We settled here in 1931.
Your humble servants, poor unfortunate settlers of Packington, county of Temiscouata.
The following is a letter from St. Benoit de Packington:
Mr. J. F. Pouliot, M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-
I am a poor settler, of 1931, in distress; however, I am not the only one. The colonization agent contends that I am the person who carries on all correspondence and criticizes the government's policy.
It is the first letter which I have received from this gentleman.
I am very sorry-I am simply doing this to prevent myself from starving to death. I have just been informed that I shall be given no further assistance, because I have requested an inquiry at home. I have clear proofs. As you will note, it is impossible for us to complain and make known our condition, because, if we do so, assistance is cut off. I bore no ill-feeling against anybody when I took such a step, I simply did so, to give bread to my family; we are nine at the table.

Would you be so kind as to advise me, for I am disheartened. I read in La Presse of Montreal of March 21, 1933, that you have espoused the cause of the poor unfortunate settlers. May I congratulate you, my comrades associate themselves with me in sincerely congratulating you.
May I, sir, inform you, that all these marks of appreciation bestowed upon me by these poor people in distress amply repays me for all the insults, aspersions and jeers that may have or may be later levelled at me by members who sit on your right, sir.
What you state in La Presse is the truth, the whole truth, nothing but the truth. What we request of you, again, is to obtain an inquiry at domicile, at Packington, county of Temiscouata, ranges eighth and ninth, south of the church. While waiting for that inquiry, we are wondering what we shall do to keep ourselves from starving to death. Have no hesitation in reading, in the house, the two letters forwarded to you, and have them also published in the newspapers.
Send us a person, with a Bible, to hold the inquiry at domicile, one who may request an oath from us but not one to hold the inquiry at the priest's house-it is not in the latter place that one sees the distress of mothers and their children.
In this connection, I think the man exaggerates, for most of the people who devote their time to settlers are absolutely impartial and I wish to give credit to the parish priests of Canada, who carry on such admirable work in promoting colonization. Furthermore, my complaints were not directed against any member of the clergy, as such, but I denounced the erroneous reports of certain provincial government officials.
Another letter is as follows:
Isle-Verte, April 5, 1933. Mr. Jean-Frangois Pouliot,
House of Commons,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-
After passing many restless nights, I decided' to write to you. The other day in reading over the newspapers, I saw that the latter endeavoured to convey that you were mistaken instating that settlers had undergone hardships. Do not allow yourself to be nonplussed. N. . . D. . . has just told my husband, in my presence,, that had he not assisted his brother-in-law- who owns a lot-and his family, they would have starved to death; when food was placed before the children, they burst into tears with their mother. They had been living for three weeks on Swedish turnips.
It is not much better than onions.
The son of M. . . D. . , recently married, after three months' residence on his lot, some people came to call on him from l'lsle-Verte. When they were about to leave the house, his young

Settlers in Rouyn District
wife got into the carriage, saying:	"I am
going back home, before I starve to death-notwithstanding the plea of her husband begging her to stay with him. That is a fact.
These, sir, are a few of the letters which I have received, a few samples only. I could quote others, I simply wished, however, to put these facts before the house, in order to prove that when I denounced certain abuses, under my responsibility as member of parliament, I deserved a better treatment than the insults, aspersions and jeers of members opposite; moreover, I should have been able to depend on their closest, constant and sincerest co-operation.
May I before closing my remarks, quote a letter of an eminent member of the clergy- he uses the third personal pronoun in writing to me:
He thanks you for your information. It is evident that we lack direction and organization, that splendid examples of devotion to duty are entirely lost by being isolated, that considerable sums of money are wasted, that colonization is carried on in regions which are not ready for settlers, that the settler himself is not taken care of in the present crisis and that this is a great national, social and religious misfortune.
Another eminent member of the clergy wrote to me on March 29, 1933, on the same date as the settler from St. Benoit-de-Packing-ton wrote to me to inform me of his distress.
The struggle wears one down, but it ends by helping one out. Be courageous!
This testimonial amply compensates me for the insults, aspersions and jeers coming from the opposite side, when the members who look after the patronage, who are influential with the government, should themselves be the ones to act and relieve the distress of these poor settlers.
The following is a letter which I received from a dignitary of the church, a pioneer of colonization, it is dated April 2, 1933.
Your reply to one of the heads of the back to the land movement would call for more than a passing remark.
I only wish to dwell, for the present on the following: "The preparation both for the future and present of all schemes, as well as all measures must be based on experience and good common sense." Few possess experience in matters of colonization. As to good common sense everybody claims it.
Will the gathering around a table, of those who are interested in settling Canadians in this country, to discuss thoroughly the problem of back to the land, etc., solve the problem?
Likely so.
But around the table, one must not only group missionary agents of colonization and a few other known authorities, whatever may be their knowledge and moral authority. The colonization problem although a social and national one, is also a political problem.
Among the voluminous correspondence received, sir, I have but two more letters to submit to the house.
A number of members may think or imagine that I am not in earnest when discussing the subject, but, I wish to point out to them that it is a crime to allow people of our race to die of hunger.
Some hon. MEMBERS (Text):	Hurrah!

speechtext:
I see those yellow creatures, members of the Ku KIux Klan, jeering at me because I am espousing the cause of my French Canadian patriots. I take this opportunity, sir, to state that I cannot understand how members of my race can thus fraternize with members who belong to the Ku Klux Klan, and then go to their province and take part in patriotic demonstrations. I find it very strange, indeed, that in Quebec, there are some who jeer, to-day, at those who endeavour to side with the humble people, those lacking protection and in distress.
I received a letter from a patriot, who belongs to a religious order.
Your letter reached me here where we are holding lent retreats. Allow me to congratulate you on your denunciation of the shocking inertia of our province and your idea of pooling all schemes and bringing together all experts so as to build up some system. Evidently there will still remain to win over the great minister, who obstructs the way and delights in doing so.
We must begin by freeing in every part of the province, the land, the soil, the millions of acres where one can lead and help the thousands and thousands of young men who are merely waiting for something to turn up. For those who look upon money as the first and final expedient of politics, the method of building a country, in a Jean Talon style, engulfing fortunes before producing any results, would be a faux pas bound to bring on failure. Only the pressure of public opinion, the fear of disorders and a general hue and cry can compel one who takes an interest in the fate of the upper classes, but none in that of the humble people, to bestir himself a little.
You enjoy free speech on the floor of the house, people watch for every word of your open and clear cut statements, you are independent, you possess individuality and you are a good patriot, why do you not bell the cat?
I wish to bell the cows, so that it may be heard!
And "Le Droit" commenting on certain statements made in the house, ended an article as follows, quoting my statement:
God forbid, stated the member for Temis-couata, if the sacred character of the priest is attacked in the house, I shall be the first to defend it, as I have already proved it. Whoever is acquainted with Mr. Pouliot will not be astonished at such language.

These include all the documents which I intended to submit to the house. The file is far from being complete as I have piles of similar letters which I could consign to Hansard. However, I have quoted enough of them to open the eyes of those who are voluntarily blind, to open the ears of those who are voluntarily deaf, to impress upon members of Quebec, members who are broadminded and free from prejudices, upon English speaking members as well as those speaking French, upon Protestant as well as Catholic members, that the time has come to cease diverting public funds 'towards the west, without providing for Quebec's quota. The hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) succeeded in getting a great deal of information in connection with the government's policy which consisted in granting the western provinces an enormous share of the country's revenue. A large portion of the deficit announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) comes from the advances made to the west. I therefore would request all members who are broad-minded, free from prejudice and parochial ideas, who wish to see the Canadian race survive, first, to bear in mind that the French Canadians of Quebec are entitled to a place under the sun, that Quebec, one of the two provinces Which are responsible for more than two-thirds of the government's revenue, is entitled to have its quota when it is a question of relieving the humble, those who lack protection and are in distress.
I did not criticize the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) to-day as sharply as he would have deserved if, really, the Gordon scheme, to which he gave his name, was to become the salvation plank of colonization in this country. I wish to especially draw the attention of the Minister of Labour on the statement I have just made and I shall again repeat to him before closing my remarks:
I would ask the Minister of Labour to be fair enough to read the letters which I have just put on Hansard and to take cognizance of them and to see that these people who are suffering the pangs of hunger receive relief at once. I do not wish him to answer me that I must take the matter up with the provincial government. I appeal now as a representative of the people to this high court of justice, the supreme court of justice in this country. I want my people and the Canadian people generally to be treated fairly. I am sure that the minister who is a generous and big-hearted man will see to it that these people are relieved without any further delay. '

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is revenue.

It is revenue, and nothing
else. As a matter of fact this is a tax upon the poor fellow who has to pay the money. The man who is getting the money should be taxed. The minister may claim that this tax is necessary in order to obtain money but I consider it one of the most vicious forms of taxation. It is not only a nuisance tax but it is an unjust tax because nothing is given for it.

As the cheques paid to dairymen are exempted from this taxation, I appeal to the minister to exempt also the cheques paid to poultrymen. In many provinces those who keep chickens are just simply keeping a few hens, so to speak, but in the province of British Columbia chicken-raising is a highly commercialized industry. The economic condition of the poultryman in that province is even more severe than that of the dairyman. A poultryman will receive perhaps eight small cheques per month, probably totalling not more than $20. The eggs are lifted once a day or twice a week, when a receipt is given accompanied by a small interim cheque for S2 or $3. When the eggs are candled, the cheque in final payment is sent to the poultryman. The poultryman receives a greater number of small cheques than the dairyman, and I appeal to the minister to exempt these cheques from the tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have every sympathy with the poultryman but we are not prepared to make further exception, although they may be worthy of consideration.
Why the dairymen?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Because of a peculiar
practice which has obtained in the payment of

Special War Revenue Act
their accounts. Perhaps it might be better not to have any exception, but that is another matter. Once we begin to make further exceptions, the door will be opened and we will never be able to get it closed. The object we had in mind in imposing this tax was the obtaining of additional revenue. I am sure that if the poultrymen of British Columbia exercise the same mental adroitness as the hon. member for New Westminster, they will be able to devise a method which will permit them to carry on their business without paying too much in this form of taxation.

When you single out a certain
class and give them exemptions, it is only natural that others in like circumstances will object. I have received many complaints from poultrymen and organizations. If every cheque was taxed I doubt if these complaints would have been made. I think a fuller explanation is required as to why the dairymen have been exempted while the poultry-men, who receive so many small cheques, should have to pay this tax.

I would like to call the attention of the minister to the fact that in Quebec we have a large number of farmers' cooperative banks, called caisses populaires, that are run by the farmers themselves. Though I am glad to know the dairymen are exempt from the payment of tax on these small cheques, I would like to call the minister's attention to these caisses populaires, farmers' cooperative banks. Are they also to be obliged to put a stamp on each cheque, because they deal in very small amounts? These are not regular banks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The case presented by the hon. member for Bonaventure had not previously been brought to my attention. Offhand I would be inclined to think those cheques would not be subject to tax. I think the tax applies only to cheques on banks; I do not think under the Bank Act those are classed as banks, but I will look into the matter because it is entirely new to me.

I thank the minister for his answer. These banks, of course, operate under a provincial charter. They are not banks in the ordinary sense of the word; they are farmers' cooperative savings banks, caisses populaires. They are very well known; they exist in all parts of my province and are patronized solely by farmers, I think they should be exempt.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have an amendment to move to this resolution:
That paragraph 6 of the resolution to amend the Special War Revenue Act, introduced on March 21, 1933, be amended by striking out of the fourth line of subsection 2 of proposed section 77a the figure "5" and substituting therefor the figure "4," and by striking out of the fourth and fifth lines of said subsection 2 the figure "50" and substituting therefor the figure "100" in both places.
In a few words, the amendment means that the tax instead of five cents for each fifty cigarette paper tubes will be four cents for 100 cigarette paper tubes. That is to say, the leaves will foe taxed at the rate of twenty cents per 1,000 and the tubes at the rate of forty cents per 1,000.
Is that an increase or a decrease?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A decrease.
From the originally proposed tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Will that permit the industry in Montreal, which closed its doors after the change, to open again?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not disposed to take exception to the manner in which my hon. friend put his question. The industry in Montreal may have closed its doors after the tax was imposed; whether that is due to the tax itself or not is open to debate, but it was felt that perhaps the rate as originally imposed was too high and I think it was. Certainly, the relative tax as between the leaves and the tubes was not properly balanced. Now we have them in the exact proportion that they ought to have, as I understand the matter, and in the same relative proportion that obtains in the United States, that is to say, twice as much upon the tube as upon the sheet. This will mean that the man who "rolls his own" will pay a small tax, but nothing comparable to the amount of tax which is paid upon the manufactured cigarette.

Under the proposed legislation before the amendment was made, is the Minister of Finance cognizant of the change this actually brought about? I say this for this reason: the other night the hon. member for Compton, speaking in the house, stated that he was satisfied with this budget because those who were best able to pay would be taxed. I take strong exception to that statement. I do not happen to be a smoker of cigarettes, but I know what has happened. A little while ago this government reduced the excise tax on package cigarettes by five cents. The price of cigarettes in the package dropped five cents; in other words, it dropped from twenty-five cents to twenty cents a package. But after all a package of cigarettes on a pound basis is a pretty expensive smoke. Consequently, the poorer people, those who cannot afford to purchase cigarettes in packages, have two methods open to them. One is "roll your own," and the other is possibly the least known, the using of tubes. You may buy tubes in two qualities. For ten cents you could buy 500 tubes manufactured in Montreal or you might purchase a better grade at fifteen cents for 500 tubes. After this tax was imposed, the price of tubes increased to 50 cents for 500 tubes and for the better class 60 cents for 500 tubes, and as a matter of fact the company stopped operating.
I am pleased at the proposed reduction but it is a pretty hard way to apply a tax when you reduce the taxes, which will favour possibly only two immense trusts in Canada and you tax the man who wants to economize or who cannot afford to smoke cigarettes in any other way, that is, the man who buys his cigarette- paper and "rolls his own," or the man who buys 500 tubes, sits down at home and puts his tobacco into them in order that he may afford to smoke cigarettes the same as the other fellow.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The lowering of the tax upon manufactured cigarettes did not take effect for the purpose of benefit which might accrue to the large cigarette manufacturing establishments. My hon. friend may not have been in the house at the time, but if he will look up the records he will find that a very distinguished predecessor of mine imposed very heavy taxation on cigarettes and it was demonstrated to him within a very short period of time that the larger tax brought far less return than had the lower one.
As in every case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not necessarily. A tax may be too low, that is dealing with it purely from a revenue viewpoint, but there comes a point

Special War Revenue Act
beyond which you will get less revenue than you will at the lower figure. It was our belief that we had taxed cigarettes to the point where we were getting a lower yield. It is too soon yet to know and we are operating in times which are not normal, so we cannot measure by normal standards what the yield is, but it is our belief that under the lower cigarette duty we shall get a higher yield to the treasury than obtained under the higher rate.
Coming to the question of the unfairness of taxing the man who "rolls his own," even after these taxes are imposed he will be able to have his cigarettes for just a trifle over one-half of the cost of them to the man who purchases the manufactured cigarettes. There is nothing comparable in the amount of return to the treasury as between the tax imposed upon the man who "rolls his own" and the man who buys his cigarettes. This principle has been recognized as fair. It would be manifestly unfair that the cigarette which pays a large return to the treasury should be diminished in its use because of permission to the smoker who rolls his own to purchase without the payment of a tax. In the United States they have resorted to this form of taxation. It is hardly necessary for me to say to my hon. friend that our only reason for imposing this tax is the need for revenue. We are certainly not imposing it, nor have we imposed any others, because we expect thereby to add to our popularity as a government.

I am exceedingly pleased
with the explanation which the minister has given. Following up that same line of argument the Finance minister will find that following the two or three budgets preceding this one, not only was the revenue diminished but it dropped practically to nothing due to the extremely high tariffs imposed by those budgets. The Minister of Finance admits that that is the case and that if you reduce the tax to the large concerns it will lessen the cost of cigarettes, and naturally increase the revenue. The Finance minister must admit that one of the reasons for the decreased general revenue is that the tariffs have been carried too high. I admit that that is not the only reason because business has been falling off and there has been a lessening of purchasing power. I am not objecting to this particular tax from the revenue standpoint, but I do not think you should put so heavy a tax on the poor man. The Finance minister admits by bringing in this amendment that the tax was too high in the first place. He has reduced it a little, which I approve of, but I do not think he should tax the fellow who is
willing to do his own cigarette manufacturing to help himself along. When the five cent excise tax was removed from the package of cigarettes the consumption of cigarettes increased for a little while and all the newspapers of the country broadcast what a wonderful thing had been done in that way in increasing the consumption of cigarettes; but if you will look at the papers for the last two or three weeks you will see that the consumption of cigarettes has decreased enormously and possibly the results have not been what the minister expected. Now on top of that you impose this immense tax on the home-made cigarette. I object to the tax because it is taxing the wrong people. It is following exactly the opposite policy enunciated in speeches made on the other side of the house that this budget was taxing those best able to pay.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
To the earlier remark of
my hon. friend I take no exception, but he must remember this, that there may be two objects in mind with respect to tariffs; one may be revenue, the other protection, or a combination of both, which is an entirely different matter from the question of raising revenue qua revenue. My hon. friend speaks, and I do not find fault with him for doing so, on behalf of the poor man who rolls his own, but even after this tax is imposed the man who rolls his own will pay $3.40 per thousand less to the treasury than the man who buys manufactured cigarettes, so he still has a very wide margin as compared with the man who buys the manufactured cigarette and who will have to pay one cent apiece.

For that I am truly thankful, and I am sorry the minister did not go further. The figures which he quoted on a previous item go to show that excessive taxation or high protection cause not only a loss of revenue but an enormous decrease in employment. I shall not read the figures which the minister gave, but that is very important. My objection is not from the revenue standpoint because I realize that we have to have revenue, but I object to taxing the man who is least able to pay.

I am sorry I was not here when the minister gave his explanation regarding stamps on cheques. I presume that the method now followed whereby one is able to use a postage stamp on a cheque will be continued.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Has any separate account been kept of the postage stamps used in that
Special War Revenue Act

way for excise purposes? The postal service is of universal use, and we are all interested in getting as cheap postage as possible, and if the revenues of the Post Office Department are increased by the use of postage stamps on cheques, it would be a good thing for us to know just what amount that represents.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is no possibility of
making a return of that.
Could not the banks do it?

If the banks could be

I say quite frankly to the committee that if I were imposing that tax as a new tax I would certainly insist upon a specific revenue stamp being used, and the postage stamp not being used, largely for the purpose of earmarking the amount and volume and incidence of the tax. But it is quite another thing when the public have become accustomed for a number of years to the use of a postage stamp. They would regard it as a real grievance now if such a change were to be made, and for this reason it was felt that it would be unwise to make it. There is no possible means of our knowing just what the proportion is, but of course to the extent that postage stamps are used, to that extent the revenue of the post office is augmented.

I wonder if the minister
could tell the committee what the estimate of the department is of the revenue to be derived from the stamp tax on cheques of five dollars and under.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have not an exact
estimate, and one of the reasons why it is difficult to find out exactly is because of the very condition referred to by my hon. friend from Bonaventure, that a proportion of the stamps used are postage stamps.

Following up what my hon. friend from Bonaventure has said, I think it is important that the government should know how much money they get in from that tax. I am not objecting to the tax, although I had hoped that the government would not find it necessary to continue it, but I do think that at the end of the year we should be able to know how much has been derived from it so that we can judge whether or not the nuisance that is created by it is compensated for by the revenue derived. I would like to know from the minister whether that could be checked so that when we come back next year we shall be able to see how much IMr. Mareil.]
the tax has brought in. It may have an important bearing on the question whether the tax should be continued.

speechtext:
I am sorry I have not
segregated figures of the estimates of the department relating to that tax. The figure given to me as the yield of the tax from stamps on cheques, drafts, promissory notes and stock transfers-for the same stamp is used for all purposes-is $2,000,000.
The minister has no idea as to the proportions-

It is unfortunate we are not using a specific stamp for this purpose. If we idid we would ibe able to tell to the>

I hope this bombardment will not induce the minister to issue excise stamps. It is very handy to be able to affix a postage stamp to a small document. If we must affix stamps, for heaven's sake let us use postage stamps, rather than have to go here and there looking for excise stamps. Even if we cannot trace the exact revenue to each department, my hope is that we will be allowed to use postage stamps.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: May I ask if maple sugar will be taxed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

Is granulated sugar, the
kind used ordinarily, still taxed at the rate of 2 cents per pound?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

was?

Will the minister tell us
what was the idea of leaving that tax of 2 cents and reducing the tax from 50 cents to 20 cents per pound on malt syrup, malt syrup powder, extract of malt or other malt products suitable for the brewing of beer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That has no relation to
sugar; I do not quite understand my hon. friend's question. Malt syrup sold, and I think still sells, at 20 cents a pound. The tax brought down in the budget was 50 cents per pound, which increased the price to the

Special War Revenue Act
point where it was excessively burdensome to those who had been accustomed to the use of malt syrup; in fact the assertion was made that it was prohibitive. There is a school of thought which believes that it would be a good thing if this tax were made prohibitive; I have had many representations of that character. On the other hand there is a school of thought which believes that because it has not been taxed hitherto it should continue to be tax free. We have steered what I hope will be a reasonably fair middle course between those two extreme points of view.
I may say that I received several deputations representing all shades of business and social activity having association with the manufacture and use of the ingredients which go into home brew.

Were the brewers among
them?
Were the consumers listened to?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, from the earnestness
with which many of the representations were made to me I took it that the gentlemen making them were reverential consumers. I may point out that in the opinion of the officials of the excise department two pounds of malt syrup would make four gallons of beer.
They do not know what they are talking about.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps my hon. friend
will be patient for a moment. Those who are iu business manufacturing and selling these products told me that this amount would make a rather thin beer, but they did say that you could safely figure on three and a half gallons from two pounds of malt syrup. Naturally they were pleading for their cause, so I thought that by splitting the difference between the two points of view I would come to a fairly accurate result. But taking the figure as given to me by those who manufacture and sell the ingredients for home brew, this is how it works out. A gallon of home brew beer will cost 22-9 cents after all costs are paid, ingredients and tax; whereas to-day the brewer pays to the federal treasury alone 26 cents per gallon. In other words, the man who makes home brew and pays the tax proposed in the amendment will be actually getting his beer per gallon at a cost to him of 3 1/10 cents less per gallon than the brewer pays in taxation to the dominion treasury alone.

Is that to encourage home
industry?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I know my hon. friend's
levity, but we must bear this in mind, that there are hundreds of thousands, I am safe in saying, certainly between one and two hundred thousand people in Canada who have been in the habit of making home brew.
Two hundred thousand in Ontario alone.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am glad to see that I
am under rather than over the mark. Through the years this has become an established practice and naturally to such people this tax will come as more or less a burden. But in these pressing times, when the treasury is in dire need of every penny it can reasonably secure in the form of taxation, it is felt to be only fair that inasmuch as the beer manufacturer pays an extremely heavy tax, a relatively modest tax should be paid by the consumer of home brew.

The first item in this schedule has been amended, but so far as granulated white sugar is concerned the tax still stands at 2 cents per pound. I want to protest in the strongest words I can use against this tax of 2 cents per pound on granulated white sugar, a commodity which perhaps is in greater demand than most any other product in Canada. At least, it has a wider distribution than any other product I know of. The tax is an enormous one, but that is not the most serious aspect of the situation; there is something else to which I wish to direct the attention of the committee, because I cannot believe that the Minister of Finance can have no knowledge at all of what I am going to disclose to-day on the floor of this house.
I was in this house a few years ago when from this side, by hon. gentlemen now opposite, an attack was made against a personal friend of mine, a minister of the crown in the Mackenzie King government, and a man who was probably as well loved as any minister has ever been in Quebec. I refer to the matter of the customs scandal and the attack made against the late Hon. George Boivin. I sat through that session and heard a two hour speech in which that gentleman was attacked, but the situation then was of minor importance compared to that which exists to-day in connection with the imposition of this sugar tax. I do not want to suggest, so far as this government is concerned, that there have been any leaks from cabinet council, because the proceedings in council are sacred. I would not suggest that any information leaked out from the cabinet so that people outside were able to discover that the tax would be imposed. But I will say that the sugar refiner-
Special War Revenue Act

ies in Canada, thirty days previous to the bringing down of the budget, were stocked with sugar; their storage houses were filled and other places were filled to overflowing with bags of granulated sugar, which was being absorbed very slowly by the consuming public because of the low purchasing power. Shortly before the budget was brought down, quite suddenly this sugar started to leave the refineries and warehouses, finding its way into the hands of wholesalers throughout the length and breadth of Canada, so much so that one concern in Montreal is rumoured to have taken 70,000 bags on which in twenty minutes it made a profit of 1140,000. You can go to every city of Canada, to the wholesalers and the wholesale grocery men of the country, and you will find that these wholesalers were tipped off, and that carloads of sugar had been shipped to them prior to the budget.
Trainloads.

I will go further than that. The day before the budget was delivered, in the city of Montreal alone, on St. Paul street, they could not get motor trucks enough to take the sugar out of the refineries and so they hired taxicabs to haul away the commodity from the refineries to the wholesalers.
Now, when we are feeding, in my constituency, 4,000 people; when we find conditions there such as we have never known in the history of Canada; when one had come to the conclusion that owing to extraordinary overcapitalization and frenzied finance in this country our financial concerns should at least have come to their senses, one does think that the ordinary citizens of Canada, the ordinary manufacturers and the common people should have been given a chance to get on their feet again and at any rate to get three meals a day before this new profiteering should occur. But right at this moment we find one concern making a net profit in twenty minutes of over $100,000. I am not finding fault so much with the profit, but I am pointing out that this tax was put on to bring revenues into the treasury of Canada, and the poor people and the masses of this country the day after the budget came down paid $2.50 per bag more; yet the money did not find its way into the coffers of th* government but into the pockets of a few.

Will the hon. gentleman
permit a question?

This matter is most
serious, Mr. Chairman. The newspapers of Canada the next day stated that over $5,000,000 would go into the pockets of a few people instead of finding its way into the treasury of the country. As a matter of fact, the taxpayers are paying $2.75 a bag more to-day, and they are taking this money from sources which are practically depleted. But they must have white sugar and so they have to pay the price. But that money is not going into the treasury of Canada. I think it would be well for the government to make the tax retroactive over a period of thirty days, but there is a better suggestion I would offer. I think it is due to the people of this country that the names of those who took this sugar out of the warehouses in the manner I have described should be published in the newspapers so that the people of Canada would know who they were. Possibly in that way we could find out how the information leaked out that this government was going to place a tax of 2 cents a pound on sugar. They are taking it from the poor people and putting it into the hands of those who after all are most responsible for the crisis we are now facing. I claim that this is a worse situation than that of keeping a poor fellow out of gaol after the warrant for arrest has-been issued; it is worse than asking that sentence be suspended temporarily. The government should inform this house before the close of this session as to just exactly what happened in connection with sugar and why the information got out. I do not like to impute wrong motives to people but let me say this-
No?
No, I d<3 not; I want to-be fair.
That is your reputation !

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Hon. members should address the chair.

I know of one company
in Montreal who are in the habit of buying sugar in 200 bag lots. As soon as one par-

Special War Revenue Act
ticular lot is disposed of they buy another batch. It happened that two days before the budget came down they placed their regular order for 200 bags of sugar. Although the refinery knew quantities of sugar were in their warehouse; they said that they could not fill the order until after a certain date, mentioning the date the budget was delivered in this house. That order for 200 bags of sugar was turned down because the refineries were oversold. Those of us who are acquainted with merchandising know that when prices are falling it is impossible to get people to buy, but once they begin to advance it is extraordinary how people will step in and buy. I do not want to make charges which cannot be substantiated but the fact remains that when this tax was placed upon sugar the natural result was that the price started to advance. It not only advanced the amount of the tax, but it went up an extra half cent per pound to cover the increased capital outlay Let us take another industry as an example. This is the way business has been done for years in the flour industry.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I do not think flour
would be covered by this item.
Forget about it.

I was just demonstrating
my point.

Go on.
Mr. HOWARD [DOT] I will continue with sugar. When the price of sugar drops, the travellers go all over the country but find they cannot place an order. Then they go around and say that sugar is going to advance a quarter of a cent per pound and they are able to take order after order. I would not like to say that this was a scheme to clean out the stocks of sugar and put them in the hands of the consumer but when the revenues of this country have been robbed of hundreds of thousands of dollars, I think it is the duty of the Minister of Finance either to make the tax retroactive for thirty days or investigate this matter most fully. This investigation should not be carried on by a commission-we have had plenty of commissions-it should be conducted by the members of this house or the members of this government. We should be informed exactly as to what happened in connection with this tax. When the people who can ill afford to pay a tax have to pay a tax on sugar, they want to be able to feel sure that the money goes into the coffers of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not
know that I can complain at the castigation that the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard) has given to certain interests in this country who were no doubt able to reap a profit as a result of the tax imposed upon sugar. Even in the case of the very best intentioned individual, a situation might arise where he would have in his possession a commodity upon which a tax had been imposed.
As far as the question of a leak is concerned, I may say that I have been at pains to make as careful an inquiry as I possibly could. I have yet to find the faintest shade, shadow or scintilla of evidence that there was anything in the nature of a leak. My hon. friend smiles, but let me give him my side of the story. Let me say to him, to any hon. member of this committee or to any person in this country, that I will welcome any information which will be kept in the utmost confidence which will put me upon the trail of any evidence to show that there was a leak with respect to the tax upon sugar. If hon. members will recall the press notices they will remember that for days prior to the budget there were all kinds of speculation as to this, that, and the other tax. Sugar was mentioned in the press several days before the government had decided to put a tax upon that commodity. I canvassed this matter within myself, if I may use that expression, for days and days and I broached it only to the officials of the department whose integrity and honour are beyond question. The matter was not mentioned even to my colleagues until a very short time before the date of the budget and the question of the rate was not determined until a few hours before the budget. I refuse to believe that there was a leak. There is no doubt there was shrewd guessing because the country realized that we were sorely put to it to secure additional revenue in an endeavour to balance our budget upon current account. The best evidence of this that I can give to the committee is a transaction which came to my notice. At the same time the press was forecasting a tax upon sugar, it forecast a tax upon tea and coffee.

Nobody loaded up
with those.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend is entirely
mistaken. I have positive evidence of one firm in the city of Winnipeg that borrowed $18,000 from the bank in order to take tea and coffee out of bond in the belief that they would be able to reap the same benefit as did those
Special War Revenue Act

who had sugar in their possession. But they lost. There are dozens and dozens of cases like that throughout the country. My hon. friend shakes his head, but I know whereof I speak.
They did not lose anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They did lose. They did
not reap their expectations and they lost to the extent of the carrying charges and the interest on the $18,000 borrowed from the bank. They also have tea and coffee upon their hands which they cannot dispose of. They are actually a substantial sum of money out of pocket. I make reference to this in order to show that the same practice obtained with respect to tea and coffee.
Not to the same extent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member may
know all about it but perhaps he will give me the right of expressing my view. I hope that is not too much to expect. I have discussed this matter with officials in other countries and it has been the subject of discussion in Great Britain for years. That is as to wrhether a method could be devised which could prevent forestalling, and with all their shrewdness, ingenuity and experience as administrators, the people of the mother country have had to admit that there is no way whereby they can prevent this.
Let me say to the hon. member for Sherbrooke and the committee that there were many business men of integrity who had no idea of loading up with sugar for the purpose of evading the payment of a tax or of making a profit. My hon. friend smiles. I am not suggesting that there were not many who did so load up, but there were in this country honest men, good intentioned citizens who did not. I make that statement merely to lead up to this: I know of my experience in this city of housewives who, having read in the press that there was going to be a tax on sugar, went down to their grocers and ordered in lots of 100, 200 and as high as 300 pounds in individual cases of which I am aware. That being so, I have, I think, every right fairly to assume that if that obtained in Ottawa, it obtained throughout Canada and as a result of that, the multiplicity of those orders made for a market stimulation in orders upon the wholesaler and by him in turn upon the sugar refiner, so that that was a contributing factor, although I do not intend to assert to how large an extent it applied.

Will my hon. friend
permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am speaking without
notes and I would like first to express one or two ideas. If my hon. friend does not mind, I would be glad if he would submit his question later.
Another factor which must be borne in mind is a fact which can be verified by access to the records. The hon. member for Sherbrooke says that when the price is going down, people do not buy, but when it is going up, they do. If my hon. friend will look at the records, he will find that there was an increase of ten cents a hundred pounds in the price of raw sugar just a few hours before the budget was delivered. That increase -had the same effect my hon. friend said it would have; when raw sugar went up, people immediately rushed to buy the granulated. That is the invariable practice in the sugar business and it so chanced that that is exactly what happened; my word need not be taken for it; the records will dislcose it to have been the case. But let me say this to my hon. friend and to the committee; if any method can be devised which will enable the government to put into the treasury money which ought properly to go there, I would welcome suggestions along that line.
The hon. member has spoken of the amount of loss. If we bear in mind the situation of which I spoke, of the stimulation in the purchase of sugar by the acceleration of orders through the retailers and wholesalers, owing to the attitude of the housewife alone, and the accumulation of those various factors, after very careful investigation and computation on the part of the Department of National Revenue, the estimate which they make is that the net loss of revenue to the treasury is ten per cent. In other words, if the yield from the sugar tax were to be $20,000,000, which is a larger figure than was anticipated, the net loss to the treasury would be $2,000,000. But my hon. friend must also bear this in mind; if a method could be devised which would enable the treasury to go out and secure that two cents per pound tax, some day-and I hope soon-the sugar tax will come off. When it does, the treasury must be prepared to hand two cents to everybody in the country who has a pound of sugar in his possession. There is no question that when the tax comes off, those who still continue in the business will make their contribution to the extent of their stocks on hand; that is the invariable experience. It is true there is never an exact balance, but

Special War Revenue Act
there is no doubt that there will be a compensating feature through the situation when the tax comes off.
The government, in imposing this tax, was under no illusion that it was going to add to its popularity.
Why did you do it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Because we had a full sense of appreciation of our duty to the people of this country including the very people who complain about the two cent tax. If the credit of Canada were impaired as a result of the negligence of the government in properly administering the finances of the country, the cost to the people ultimately would be far greater than two cents a pound on sugar.
Why place the tax on the poor fellow all the time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The tax was imposed, as the committee well knows, solely because of the dire necessity for revenue. It may be a new experience to certain people in this country that a revenue tax of this character should be imposed, but it is not new in other countries. In the mother country for many years they have had similar taxes on many commodities, and the people have paid them, perhaps grudgingly in many instances, knowing the treasury had to have the revenue. But it must be borne in mind that even with the price of sugar as it is to-day and with the tax added, the householder can purchase sugar at a far lower price than the average which has ruled over the last twenty years.
But these are times of depression.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I quite appreciate that; we all realize it, and I might counter by sayinng that if it were not for the conditions in which we live, we would not be imposing a sugar tax. We are living in an unusual period in the world's history and we must resort in some instances to unusual methods to attempt to cope with conditions. It is sad that at a period when the government has to tax most, the people are least in a position to pay. That is one of the very regrettable features; nobody deplores this more than I do, but we would be doing a disservice to the people if we did not protect the financial credit of the country through taxation.
But we should not protect the profiteers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend, and if there were any method by which we could get at the profiteers, I would be the first to say that we should do so.
At what time did the tax become effective on granulated sugar?

speechtext: I am unable to give my hon. friend an accurate answer, but three or four days ago I observed in a paper published in the constituency of my hon. friend from Hants-Kings, the WTindsor Tribune, that in Newport in that county sugar was selling at ten pounds for 65 cents, and I observed that A. Let us assume that the price is 7 cents.
In New York you can buy ten pounds for 40 cents.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not suggesting that that may not be so, but I am not dealing with New York but with Canada, and with the price in Canada to-day as compared with the last twenty years. So even with the tax added, the price of sugar to-day is much less than the average prevailing price for the last twenty years. Having that in mind and having regard to the conditions, I do say that the tax ought not to be regarded as unduly burdensome. I have spoken at greater length than I had intended, and I hope hon. gentlemen will forgive me for not having answered any questions which they wished to put to me while I was on my feet, but to the best of my ability I shall endeavour to answer them as they submit them now.

The minister cited the fact that householders had purchased sugar on the assumption perhaps that there would be a tax on sugar. We are not complaining about the householders. They were not going to sell sugar and make a profit out of it; it was for their own use in their own household. What we criticize is the fact that in some way or other information got out to certain people, and they purchased sugar before the tax came into effect, and reaped large profits.
My hon. friend from Sherbrooke has spoken of Montreal. There is a rumour

I do not know whether it is correct or not-which the Minister of Finance may have heard, and at least when it reaches his ears he should investigate it, that one brokerage firm in the city of Toronto by some means or other got information which they said was absolutely authentic, and on that information they went to their bankers and the result was

that they purchased, not carloads, but trainloads of sugar, and it is reported that their profit was as much as $2,000,000. When I say brokerage firm, I do not mean grocery brokerage but the old-fashioned kind of brokers who used to make money when stocks were being bought and sold. I do not know whether this rumour is correct or not. Nevertheless, even if their profit was $100 instead of $2,000,000, if it was obtained through getting inside information and they purchased to avoid paying the government the tax that was due, the -matter should be investigated, ahd if it is true these people should be prosecuted. There is no comparison between the broker or gambler or speculator who buys sugar and sells it and the householder who buys a few pounds of sugar for use in her own home. I say in all seriousness, and I believe the minister is serious over this and would be glad to get any information he can in regard to it, that he should search diligently to find the source of the leak. For the good of the tax-payers of this country the minister should not let this question rest with this debate, but he should get busy and get his officials busy and try to get some authentic information. I think he will find that the rumours in some degree are correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend must not think that when I made reference to the individual householder I was for one moment suggesting that there was anything wrong in what that householder did, nor was I complaining in the slightest degree. If my hon. friend had followed me he would have realized that I -merely referred to that incident for one purpose and one purpose only. I said that the multiplication of these cases would account for a substantial part of the accelerated movement of sugar prior to the imposition of the tax, and I think that is a fair assumption. I am not complaining of that at all, nor do I complain at the castigation which my hon. friend would give anybody who would profiteer under those conditions at the expense of the people of this country and of the treasury. I have not heard of the incident referred to by my hon. friend. I welcome any information that could be given to me. I may say to him that the officials of the Department of National Revenue have made a check-up in every refinery in Canada and there is absolutely no evidence upon the records of business that any such transaction did take place or could have taken place because the sales were

Special War Revenue Act
all made to the usual customers and the usual dealers who are purchasers of sugar, and unless one of these had become a party to a transaction of that character there could be no truth in the statement. Certainly there could be no truth in the statement so far as the magnitude of the transaction mentioned by my hon. friend is concerned. I hope that my hon. friend will not for one moment think that we want to fold our arms peacefully and say that this incident is closed-not at all.
I am very sincerely desirous, naturally as Minister of Finance, apart from any other consideration, because of the loss to the treasury that the treasury should be recouped to the last farthing if possible. But a pious desire to do so and a method of doing so without doing injustice is another thing. You cannot follow a pound of sugar very well after it has left-
Mr. SANDEiRSON:	The minister might
follow a trainload.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The figures which I gave before to the committee are accurate. They are the result of an actual computation made from the books of the refineries themselves, that the maximum amount that could have been lost to the treasury is $2,000,000.
That would be one million bags.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Quite so, but my hon. friend from South Perth referred to a firm of brokers in Toronto who are said to have purchased trainloads of sugar. There was an acceleration of sugar purchases throughout the whole dominion, but there was not enough sugar loose in the land for trainloads to be put up under those conditions. I repeat that hon. gentlemen owe it as a duty to themselves, to their constituents and the country-rumour and suspicion and that sort of thing is worthless-but if they can get any evidence, which I very much doubt that there was anything in the nature of a leak I shall be glad to get it.

I appreciate that the Minister of Finance wants to get all the revenue he can, and that is the reason I put the facts before the committee as I did this afternoon. There are two ways in which it could be done. First of all, I think the minister will admit that if a person had been .buying sugar from the refinery as he needed it in carload lots, and then all of a sudden pur-53719-273
chased ten cars at one time there must have been something extraordinarily wrong. Those things do not just happen. There are two ways of meeting the difficulty. I have already suggested that the provision should be made retroactive for thirty days from the date of the budget. In that way the minister would not be inflicting any hardship on anybody. The householder or consumer who has purchased a bag of sugar has paid $6.50 or $6.75 a bag for it. The only person making any money is the man who either was tipped off or took exceptionally large quantities of sugar for resale. The reason I suggest the change is that it would be in the interests of the country, and provide revenue.
We have been discussing an item to-day in regard to cigarette papers and tubes, and surely the item in regard to sugar should not be allowed to stand as it is. When the banks of the United States found that through people withdrawing gold they had practically no gold left in their vaults, the President issued a statement to the effect that unless the gold were put back into the banks within a week's time he would publish the names of the people who had taken it out. What happened? The gold came back mighty quickly. Why not use this publicity method.
There are many ways of meeting the difficulty this item presents. If the treasury of Canada can get back $2,000,000 from people who had no right to make excess profits in these times, then .that would be the wise thing to do, and would be a good deal better than just imposing the tax for which provision is made. I have nothing to say concerning the minister's suggestion, except that according to his figures the average price of sugar was 9-2 cents per pound, while to-day it is only 6-75. Any person in Canada will admit that 6-75 cents is much .more to-day than 9-2 was at an earlier period. We must consider present purchasing power.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I hope the hon. member for Sherbrooke will not object to a question. He has stated that the tax should be made retroactive for thirty days. From whom would he collect that tax?

From the wholesalers who purchased the sugar. The refinery in Canada which takes sugar cane from the south or sugar beets from our fields and converts it into sugar does not sell that sugar to the householder or to the consumer. That is not done. That sugar goes through the regular

Special War Revenue Act

channels of business into the hands of the wholesalers and from the wholesalers to retailers then to the consumer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member has suggested that for a period of thirty days prior to March 21, he would impose a tax of 2 cents a pound upon all sugar sold by wholesalers. Is that correct?
I did not say that.
You did.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What did you say?

I shall repeat it. Either the Minister of Finance or the Minister of National Revenue upon looking into the books of refineries could tell exactly who bought the sugar. They could go back six months and find out how much sugar each firm took in that time. When he finds that the wholesaler has purchased not twice or three times the regular monthly quantity, but that he has purchased from ten to twenty times that quantity, he should ask that wholesaler to pay a tax on the increased quantity of sugar. As I have suggested it was bought because of information received, or for some other reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I understood the hon.
member to state very distinctly that he would collect from the wholesalers.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Yes, and then you would not have to investigate.

My hon. friend said that.

How will the hon. member establish a definition for the term "normal purchase." They could not do it in England -but of course we are much brighter here!

Certainly we have not had the same amount of experience. Who will determine what is a normal purchase on the part of a wholesaler?

stock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why does the hon. member smile, if he feels that way? I assure you I do not feel like smiling. The sugar tax is a very serious business; it is not nearly as sweet as it sounds. We are not concerned with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I know we are not. My
hon. friend is too bright to allow his mind to be clouded with the thought that I am criticizing the householder. I am not doing that. I am referring to an accumulation of orders, and am not saying that it was not a perfectly proper procedure for the housewife to take. But those orders banked up. If the local grocer's stock is depleted he calls up the wholesaler, and if those orders are multiplied there is sure to be an accumulation. The wholesaler would sell it in the ordinary course of business. The hon. member for Sherbrooke would turn around and make the poor unfortunate wholesaler pay two cents a pound on sugar which he had sold in good faith to the local grocer, and on sales which were brought about by accelerated orders.
I do not believe there is any one commodity in Canada which through a period of years has uniformly yielded such a small profit as has sugar.

given an opportunity to say a word in answer. If the minister misunderstood me I am sorry;
